entries.c63387caabceb8a754c9c8eed444a3b7fcfd21c8: <div sID="gen5704" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="1Sam.21" sID="1Sam.21"/> <div eID="gen5704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5705" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5706" type="x-p"/> David has now quite taken leave both of Saul's court and of his camp, has bidden farewell to his alter idem—his other self, the beloved Jonathan; and henceforward to the end of this book he is looked upon and treated as an outlaw and proclaimed a traitor. We still find him shifting from place to place for his own safety, and Saul pursuing him. His troubles are very particularly related in this and the following chapters, not only to be a key to the Psalms, but that he might be, as other prophets, an example to the saints in all ages, "of suffering affliction, and of patience," and especially that he might be a type of Christ, who, being anointed to the kingdom, humbled himself, and was therefore highly exalted. But the example of the suffering Jesus was a copy without a blot, that of David was not so; witness the records of this chapter, where we find David in his flight, I. Imposing upon Abimelech the priest, to get from him both victuals and arms, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. Imposing upon Achish, king of Gath, by feigning himself mad, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15">ver. 10-15</reference>. Justly are troubles called temptations, for many are by them drawn into sin.
entries.2c3e181df19ed87b8d53339c55219b37adf8f1df: <div eID="gen5706" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5705" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Obtains the Show-Bread; David Gets the Sword of Goliath. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5707" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou alone, and no man with thee? <hi type="super">2</hi> And David said unto Ahimelech the priest, The king hath commanded me a business, and hath said unto me, Let no man know any thing of the business whereabout I send thee, and what I have commanded thee: and I have appointed <hi type="italic">my</hi> servants to such and such a place. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now therefore what is under thine hand? give <hi type="italic">me</hi> five <hi type="italic">loaves of</hi> bread in mine hand, or what there is present. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the priest answered David, and said, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no common bread under mine hand, but there is hallowed bread; if the young men have kept themselves at least from women. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David answered the priest, and said unto him, Of a truth women <hi type="italic">have been</hi> kept from us about these three days, since I came out, and the vessels of the young men are holy, and <hi type="italic">the bread is</hi> in a manner common, yea, though it were sanctified this day in the vessel. <hi type="super">6</hi> So the priest gave him hallowed <hi type="italic">bread:</hi> for there was no bread there but the showbread, that was taken from before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to put hot bread in the day when it was taken away. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now a certain man of the servants of Saul <hi type="italic">was</hi> there that day, detained before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and his name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Doeg, an Edomite, the chiefest of the herdmen that <hi type="italic">belonged</hi> to Saul. <hi type="super">8</hi> And David said unto Ahimelech, And is there not here under thine hand spear or sword? for I have neither brought my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the priest said, The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom thou slewest in the valley of Elah, behold, it <hi type="italic">is here</hi> wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod: if thou wilt take that, take <hi type="italic">it:</hi> for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no other save that here. And David said, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> none like that; give it me. <div eID="gen5707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5708" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David, in distress, flies in the tabernacle of God, now pitched at Nob, supposed to be a city in the tribe of Benjamin. Since Shiloh was forsaken, the tabernacle was often removed, though the ark still remained at Kirjath-jearim. Hither David came in his flight from Saul's fury (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1">v. 1</reference>), and applied to Ahimelech the priest. Samuel the prophet could not protect him, Jonathan the prince could not. He therefore has recourse next to Ahimelech the priest. He foresees he must now be an exile, and therefore comes to the tabernacle, 1. To take an affecting leave of it, for he knows not when he shall see it again, and nothing will be more afflictive to him in his banishment than his distance from the house of God, and his restraint from public ordinances, as appears by many of his psalms. He had given an affectionate farewell to his friend Jonathan, and cannot go till he has given the like to the tabernacle. 2. To enquire of the Lord there, and to beg direction from him in the way both of duty and safety, his case being difficult and dangerous. That this was his business appears <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.10">ch. xxii. 10</reference>, where it is said that <hi type="italic">Ahimelech enquired of the Lord for him,</hi> as he had done formerly, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.15">v. 15</reference>. It is a great comfort to us in a day of trouble that we have a God to go to, to whom we may open our case, and from whom we may ask and expect direction. <div eID="gen5708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5709" type="x-p"/> II. Ahimelech the priest is surprised to see him in so poor an equipage; having heard that he had fallen into disgrace at court, he looked shy upon him, as most are apt to do upon their friends when the world frowns upon them. He was afraid of incurring Saul's displeasure by entertaining him, and took notice how mean a figure he now made to what he used to make: <hi type="italic">Why art thou alone?</hi> He had some with him (as appears <reference osisRef="Mark.2.26">Mark ii. 26</reference>), but they were only his own servants; he had none of the courtiers, no persons of quality with him, as he used to have at other times, when he came to enquire of the Lord. He says (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Ps. xlii. 4</reference>) he was wont to <hi type="italic">go with a multitude to the house of God;</hi> and, having now but two or three with him, Ahimelech might well ask, <hi type="italic">Why art thou alone?</hi> He that was suddenly advanced from the solitude of a shepherd's life to the crowd and hurries of the camp is now as soon reduced to the desolate condition of an exile and is <hi type="italic">alone like a sparrow on the housetop,</hi> such charges are there in this world and so uncertain are its smiles! Those that are courted to-day may be deserted to-morrow. <div eID="gen5709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5710" type="x-p"/> III. David, under pretence of being sent by Saul upon public services, solicits Ahimelech to supply his present wants, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.2-1Sam.21.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. <div eID="gen5710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5711" type="x-p"/> 1. Here David did not behave like himself. He told Ahimelech a gross untruth, that Saul had ordered him business to despatch, that his attendants were dismissed to such a place, and that he was charged to observe secresy and therefore durst not communicate it, no, not to the priest himself. This was all false. What shall we say to this? The scripture does not conceal it, and we dare not justify it. It was ill done, and proved of bad consequence; for it <hi type="italic">occasioned the death of the priests of the Lord,</hi> as David reflected upon it afterwards with regret, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.22">ch. xxii. 22</reference>. It was needless for him thus to dissemble with the priest, for we may suppose that, if he had told him the truth, he would have sheltered and relieved him as readily as Samuel did, and would have known the better how to advise him and enquire of God for him. People should be free with their faithful ministers. David was a man of great faith and courage, and yet now both failed him, and he fell thus foully through fear and cowardice, and both owing to the weakness of his faith. Had he trusted God aright, he would not have used such a sorry sinful shift as this for his own preservation. It is written, not for our imitation, no, not in the greatest straits, but for our admonition. <hi type="italic">Let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall;</hi> and let us all pray daily, <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation.</hi> Let us all take occasion from this to lament, (1.) The weakness and infirmity of good men; the best are not perfect on this side heaven. There may be true grace where yet there are many failings. (2.) The wickedness of bad times, which forces good men into such straits as prove temptations too strong for them. Oppression makes a wise man do foolishly. <div eID="gen5711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5712" type="x-p"/> 2. Two things David begged of Ahimelech, <hi type="italic">bread</hi> and a <hi type="italic">sword.</hi> <div eID="gen5712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5713" type="x-p"/> (1.) He wanted bread: <hi type="italic">five loaves,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.3">v. 3</reference>. Travelling was then troublesome, when men generally carried their provisions with them in kind, having little money and no public houses, else David would not now have had to seek for bread. It seems David had known the <hi type="italic">seed of the righteous begging bread</hi> occasionally, but not constantly, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.25">Ps. xxxvii. 25</reference>. Now, [1.] The priest objected that he had none but hallowed bread, <hi type="italic">show-bread,</hi> which had stood a week on the golden table in the sanctuary, and was taken thence for the use of the priests and their families, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.4">v. 4</reference>. It seems the priest kept no good house, but wanted either a heart to be hospitable or provisions wherewithal to be so. Ahimelech thinks that the young men that attended David might not eat of this bread unless they had for some time abstained from women, even from their own wives; this was required at the <hi type="italic">giving of the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.15">Exod. xix. 15</reference>), but otherwise we never find this made the matter of any ceremonial purity on the one side or pollution on the other, and therefore the priest here seems to be over-nice, not to say superstitious. [2.] David pleads that he and those that were with him, in this case of necessity, might lawfully eat of the hallowed bread, for they were not only able to answer his terms of keeping from women for three days past, but <hi type="italic">the vessels</hi> (that is, the bodies) <hi type="italic">of the young men were holy,</hi> being <hi type="italic">possessed in sanctification and honour at all times</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.4-1Thess.4.5">1 Thess. iv. 4, 5</reference>), and therefore God would take particular care of them, that they wanted not necessary supports, and would have his priest to do so. Being thus holy, holy things were not forbidden them. Poor and pious Israelites were in effect priests to God, and, rather than be starved, might feed on the bread which was appropriated to the priests. Believers are spiritual priests, and the offerings of the Lord shall be their inheritance; they eat the bread of their God. He pleads that the bread is in a manner common, now that what was primarily the religious use of it is over; especially (as our margin reads it) <hi type="italic">where there is other bread</hi> (<hi type="italic">hot,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.6">v. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">sanctified that day in the vessel,</hi> and put in the room of it upon the table. This was David's plea, and the Son of David approves it, and shows from it that mercy is to be preferred to sacrifice, that ritual observance must give way to moral duties, and that may be done in a case of an urgent providential necessity which may not otherwise be done. He brings it to justify his disciples in plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day, for which the Pharisees censured them, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.3-Matt.12.4">Matt. xii. 3, 4</reference>. [3.] Ahimelech hereupon supplies him: <hi type="italic">He gave him hallowed bread</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.6">v. 6</reference>), and some think it was about this that <hi type="italic">he enquired of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.10">ch. xxii. 10</reference>. As a faithful servant he would not dispose of his master's provisions without his master's leave. This bread, we may suppose, was the more agreeable to David for its being hallowed, so precious were all sacred things to him. The show-bread was but twelve loaves in all, yet out of these he gave David five (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.3">v. 3</reference>), though they had no more in the house; but he trusted Providence. <div eID="gen5713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5714" type="x-p"/> (2.) He wanted a sword. Persons of quality, though officers of the army, did not then wear their swords so constantly as now they do, else surely David would not have been without one. It was a wonder that Jonathan did not furnish him with his, as he had before done, <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.4">ch. xviii. 4</reference>. However, it happened that he had now no weapons with him, the reason of which he pretends to be because he came away in haste, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.8">v. 8</reference>. Those that are furnished with the sword of the Spirit and the shield of faith cannot be disarmed of them, nor need they, at any time, to be at a loss. But the priests, it seems, had no swords: the weapons of their warfare were not carnal. There was not a sword to be found about the tabernacle but the sword of Goliath, which was laid up behind the ephod, as a monument of the glorious victory David obtained over him. Probably David had an eye to that when he asked the priest to help him with a sword; for, that being mentioned, O! says he, <hi type="italic">there is none like that, give it to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">v. 9</reference>. He could not use Saul's armour, for he had not proved it; but this sword of Goliath he had made trial of and done execution with. By this it appears that he was now well grown in strength and stature, that he could wear and wield such a sword as that. God had <hi type="italic">taught his hands to war,</hi> so that he could do wonders, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.34">Ps. xviii. 34</reference>. Two things we may observe concerning this sword:—[1.] That God had graciously given it to him, as a pledge of his singular favour; so that whenever he drew it, nay, whenever he looked upon it, it would be a great support to his faith, by bringing to mind that great instance of the particular care and countenance of the divine providence respecting him. [2.] That he had gratefully given it back to God, dedicating it to him and to his honour as a token of his thankfulness; and now in his distress it stood him greatly in stead. Note, What we devote to God's praise, and serve him with, is most likely to redound, one way or other, to our own comfort and benefit. What we gave we have. <div eID="gen5714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5715" type="x-p"/> Thus was David well furnished with arms and victuals; but it fell out very unhappily that there was one of Saul's servants then attending before the Lord, <hi type="italic">Doeg</hi> by name, that proved a base traitor both to David and Ahimelech. He was by birth an Edomite (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.7">v. 7</reference>), and though proselyted to the Jewish religion, to get the preferment he now had under Saul, yet he retained the ancient and hereditary enmity of Edom to Israel. He was master of the herds, which perhaps was then a place of as much honour as master of the horse is now. Some occasion or other he had at this time to wait on the priest, either to be purified from some pollution or to pay some vow; but, whatever his business was, it is said, he was <hi type="italic">detained before the Lord.</hi> He must attend and could not help it, but he was sick of the service, <hi type="italic">snuffed at it, and said, What a weariness is it!</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.1.13">Mal. i. 13</reference>. He would rather have been any where else than before the Lord, and therefore, instead of minding the business he came about, was plotting to do David a mischief and to be revenged on Ahimelech for detaining him. God's sanctuary could never secure such wolves in sheep's clothing. See <reference osisRef="Gal.2.4">Gal. ii. 4</reference>.
entries.544280ab2c5963a1e6d40a4b71adabd0da059caa: <div eID="gen5715" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Driven from Achish. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5716" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And David arose, and fled that day for fear of Saul, and went to Achish the king of Gath. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the servants of Achish said unto him, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not this David the king of the land? did they not sing one to another of him in dances, saying, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands? <hi type="super">12</hi> And David laid up these words in his heart, and was sore afraid of Achish the king of Gath. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then said Achish unto his servants, Lo, ye see the man is mad: wherefore <hi type="italic">then</hi> have ye brought him to me? <hi type="super">15</hi> Have I need of mad men, that ye have brought this <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> to play the mad man in my presence? shall this <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> come into my house? <div eID="gen5716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5717" type="x-p"/> David, though king elect, is here an exile—designed to be master of vast treasures, yet just now begging his bread—anointed to the crown, and yet here forced to flee from his country. Thus do God's providences sometimes seem to run counter to his promises, for the trial of his people's faith, and the glorifying of his name, in the accomplishment of his counsels, notwithstanding the difficulties that lay in the way. Here is, 1. David's flight into the land of the Philistines, where he hoped to be hid, and to remain undiscovered in the court or camp of Achish king of Gath, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10">v. 10</reference>. Israel's darling is necessitated to quit the land of Israel, and he that was the Philistine's great enemy (upon I know not what inducements) goes to seek for shelter among them. It should seem that as, though the Israelites loved him, yet the king of Israel had a personal enmity to him, which obliged him to leave his own country, so, though the Philistines hated him, yet the king of Gath had a personal kindness for him, valuing his merit, and perhaps the more for his killing Goliath of Gath, who, it may be, had been no friend to Achish. To him David now went directly, as to one he could confide in, as afterwards (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2-1Sam.27.3">ch. xxvii. 2, 3</reference>), and Achish would not have protected him but that he was afraid of disobliging his own people. God's persecuted people have often found better usage from Philistines than from Israelites, in the Gentile theatres than in the Jewish synagogues. The king of Judah imprisoned Jeremiah, and the king of Babylon set him at liberty. 2. The disgust which the servants of Achish took at his being there, and their complaint of it to Achish (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Is not this David?</hi> Is not this he that has triumphed over the Philistines? witness that burden of the song which was so much talked of, <hi type="italic">Saul has slain his thousands,</hi> but <hi type="italic">David,</hi> this very man, <hi type="italic">his ten thousands.</hi> Nay, Is not this he that (if our intelligence from the land of Israel be true) is, or is to be, <hi type="italic">king of the land?</hi>" As such, "he must be an enemy to our country; and is it safe or honourable for us to protect or entertain such a man?" Achish perhaps had intimated to them that it would be policy to entertain David, because he was now an enemy to Saul, and he might be hereafter a friend to them. It is common for the outlaws of a nation to be sheltered by the enemies of that nation. But the servants of Achish objected to his politics, and thought it not at all fit that he should stay among them. 3. The fright which this put David into. Though he had some reason to put confidence in Achish, yet, when he perceived the servants of Achish jealous of him, he began to be afraid that Achish would be obliged to deliver him up to them, and he was <hi type="italic">sorely afraid</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.12">v. 12</reference>), and perhaps he was the more apprehensive of his own danger, when he was thus discovered, because he wore Goliath's sword, which, we may suppose, was well known in Gath, and with which he had reason to expect they would cut off his head, as he had cut off Goliath's with it. David now learned by experience what he has taught us (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.9">Ps. cxviii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">that it is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in princes.</hi> Men of high degree are a lie, and, if we make them our hope, they may prove our fear. It was at this time that David penned <reference osisRef="Ps.55.1-Ps.55.23">Psalm lv.</reference> (<hi type="italic">Michtam, a golden psalm), when the Philistines took him in Gath,</hi> where having shown before God his distresses, he resolves (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.3">v. 3</reference>), "<hi type="italic">What time I am afraid I will trust in thee;</hi> and therefore (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11">v. 11</reference>) <hi type="italic">will not be afraid what man can do unto me,</hi> no, not the sons of giants." 4. The course he took to get out of their hands: <hi type="italic">He feigned himself mad,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.13">v. 13</reference>. He used the gestures and fashions of a natural fool, or one that had gone out of his wits, supposing they would be ready enough to believe that the disgrace he had fallen into, and the troubles he was now in, had driven him distracted. This dissimulation of his cannot be justified (it was a mean thing thus to disparage himself, and inconsistent with truth thus to misrepresent himself, and therefore not becoming the honour and sincerity of such a man as David); yet it may in some degree be excused, for it was not a downright lie and it was like a stratagem in war, by which he imposed upon his enemies for the preservation of his own life. What David did here in pretence and for his own safety, which made it partly excusable, drunkards do really, and only to gratify a base lust: they made fools of themselves and change their behaviour; their words and actions commonly are either as silly and ridiculous as an idiot's or as furious and outrageous as a madman's, which has often made me wonder that ever men of sense and honour should allow themselves in it. 5. His escape by this means, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.14-1Sam.21.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. I am apt to think Achish was aware that the delirium was but counterfeit, but, being desirous to protect David (as we find afterwards he was very kind to him, even when the lord of the Philistines favoured him not, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1-1Sam.28.2">ch. xxviii. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.6">xxix. 6</reference>), he pretended to his servants that he really thought he was mad, and therefore had reason to question whether it was David or no; or, if it were, they need not fear him, what harm could he do them now that his reason had departed from him? They suspected that Achish was inclined to entertain him: "Not I," says he. "He is a madman. I'll have nothing to do with him. You need not fear that I should employ him, or give him any countenance." He humours the thing well enough when he asks, "<hi type="italic">Have I need of madmen?</hi> <hi type="italic">Shall this fool come into my house?</hi> I will show him no kindness, but then you shall do him no hurt, for, if he be a madmen, he is to be pitied." He therefore <hi type="italic">drove him away,</hi> as it is in the title of <reference osisRef="Ps.34.1">Ps. xxxiv.</reference>, which David penned upon this occasion, and an excellent psalm it is, and shows that he did not change his spirit when he changed his behaviour, but even in the greatest difficulties and hurries his <hi type="italic">heart was fixed,</hi> trusting in the Lord; and he concludes that psalm with this assurance, that <hi type="italic">none of those that trust in God shall be desolate,</hi> though they may be, as he now was, solitary and distressed, <hi type="italic">persecuted, but not forsaken.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Sam.21"/> <div eID="gen5717" type="x-p"/>

entries.0a34c424f569aafcd895df293bd6b95312158513: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2725"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 21</title> <div sID="gen3712" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.7">1Sa 21:1-7</reference>. David, at Nob, Obtains of Ahimelech Hallowed Bread.<div eID="gen3712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2725"/><hi type="bold">1. Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech--</hi>Nob, a city of the priests (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:19</reference>), was in the neighborhood of Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives--a little north of the top, and on the northeast of the city. It is computed to have been about five miles distant from Gibeah. Ahimelech, the same as Ahiah, or perhaps his brother, both being sons of Ahitub (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference>, with 1Sa 22:4-11, 20). His object in fleeing to this place was partly for the supply of his necessities, and partly for comfort and counsel, in the prospect of leaving the kingdom.<div eID="gen3713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David--</hi>suspecting some extraordinary occurrence by his appearing so suddenly, and in such a style, for his attendants were left at a little distance. <div eID="gen3714" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb9aecc61bf095764da347dcc0eedd41e3f2ffd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2726"/><div sID="gen3715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2726"/><hi type="bold">2. The king hath commanded me a business, and hath said unto me, Let no man know--</hi>This was a direct falsehood, extorted through fear. David probably supposed, like many other persons, that a lie is quite excusable which is told for the sole purpose of saving the speaker's life. But what is essentially sinful, can never, from circumstances, change its immoral character; and David had to repent of this vice of lying (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.29">Psa 119:29</reference>). <div eID="gen3715" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2c615a638b7477f2c1f535530f1fef9d1f7a706: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2727"/><div sID="gen3716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2727"/><hi type="bold">4. there is hallowed bread--</hi>There would be plenty of bread in his house; but there was no time to wait for it. "The hallowed bread" was the old shew-bread, which had been removed the previous day, and which was reserved for the use of the priests alone (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.9">Le 24:9</reference>). Before entertaining the idea that this bread could be lawfully given to David and his men, the high priest seems to have consulted the oracle (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.10">1Sa 22:10</reference>) as to the course to be followed in this emergency. A dispensation to use the hallowed bread was specially granted by God Himself. <div eID="gen3716" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e5c420d4dff8b4de7741cd7b610165018a5df7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2728"/><div sID="gen3717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2728"/><hi type="bold">5. these three days--</hi>as required by law (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.15">Ex 19:15</reference>). David and his attendants seem to have been lurking in some of the adjoining caves, to elude pursuit, and to have been, consequently, reduced to great extremities of hunger.<div eID="gen3717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bread is in a manner common--</hi>that is, now that it is no longer standing on the Lord's table. It is eaten by the priests, and may also, in our circumstances, be eaten by us.<div eID="gen3718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yea, though it were sanctified this day in the vessel--</hi>that is, though the hallowed bread had been but newly placed on the vessel, the ritual ordinance would have to yield to the great law of necessity and mercy (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.3">Mt 12:3</reference>; also see <reference osisRef="Mark.2.25">Mr 2:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.3">Lu 6:3</reference>). <div eID="gen3719" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc65f2bf2abd9ed0bbe692f2432f2e699c376cf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2729"/><div sID="gen3720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2729"/><hi type="bold">6. there was no bread there--</hi>in the tabernacle. The removal of the old and the substitution of the new bread was done on the Sabbath (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.8">Le 24:8</reference>), the loaves being kept warm in an oven heated the previous day. <div eID="gen3720" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b776f40b6d9764ba3fad72a4e2ee152cbf6544f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2730"/><div sID="gen3721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2730"/><hi type="bold">7. Doeg, an Edomite--</hi>who had embraced the Hebrew religion.<div eID="gen3721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">detained before the Lord--</hi>at the tabernacle, perhaps, in the performance of a vow, or from its being the Sabbath, which rendered it unlawful for him to prosecute his journey.<div eID="gen3722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the chiefest of the herdmen that belonged to Saul--</hi>Eastern monarchs anciently had large possessions in flocks and herds; and the office of the chief shepherd was an important one.<div eID="gen3723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3724" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">1Sa 21:9</reference>. He Takes Goliath's Sword. <div eID="gen3724" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca8f0f4194d3024a358f4e05745fe7063384cb3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2731"/><div sID="gen3725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2731"/><hi type="bold">9. sword of Goliath--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.54">1Sa 17:54</reference>).<div eID="gen3725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behind the ephod--</hi>in the place allowed for keeping the sacred vestments, of which the ephod is mentioned as the chief. The giant's sword was deposited in that safe custody as a memorial of the divine goodness in delivering Israel.<div eID="gen3726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">There is none like that--</hi>not only for its size and superior temper, but for its being a pledge of the divine favor to him, and a constant stimulus to his faith.<div eID="gen3727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3728" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15">1Sa 21:10-15</reference>. At Gath He Feigns Himself Mad. <div eID="gen3728" type="x-p"/>
entries.29b6520fa3c692fbbc355935a7edf8f07421ef32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2732"/><div sID="gen3729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2732"/><hi type="bold">10. David ... fled ... to Achish the king of Gath--</hi>which was one of the five principalities of the Philistines. In this place his person must have been known, and to venture into that country, he their greatest enemy, and with the sword of Goliath in his hand, would seem to have been a perilous experiment; but, doubtless, the protection he received implies that he had been directed by the divine oracle. Achish was generous (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">1Sa 27:6</reference>). He might wish to weaken the resources of Saul, and it was common in ancient times for great men to be harbored by neighboring princes. <div eID="gen3729" type="x-p"/>
entries.7233402f69b33f5d1585881636d1f5c07bcca4c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2733"/><div sID="gen3730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2733"/><hi type="bold">13. feigned himself mad--</hi>It is supposed to have been an attack of epilepsy, real or perhaps only pretended. This disease is relieved by foaming at the mouth.<div eID="gen3730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let his spittle fall down upon his beard--</hi>No wonder that Achish supposed him insane, as such an indignity, whether done by another, or one's self, to the beard, is considered in the East an intolerable insult. <chapter eID="1Sam.21"/>

entries.ea324c613188eab703a23734a93223510cb75651: <div eID="gen10314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10315" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10316" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10316" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10315" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10317" type="x-p"/> David comes to Ahimelech at Nob, receives provisions from him, and the sword of Goliath; and is noticed by Doeg, one of the servants of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.9">1Sam 21:1-9</reference>. He leaves Nob, and goes to Achish, king of Gath, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10">1Sam 21:10</reference>. But on being recognised as the vanquisher of Goliath by the servants of Achish, he feigns himself deranged, and Achish sends him away, <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11-1Sam.21.15">1Sam 21:11-15</reference>. <div eID="gen10317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10318" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10319" type="x-p"/> Then came David to Nob - There were two places of this name, one on this side, the second on the other side of Jordan; but it is generally supposed that Nob, near Gibeah of Benjamin, is the place here intended; it was about twelve miles from Jerusalem. <div eID="gen10319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10320" type="x-p"/> Why art thou alone - Ahimelech probably knew nothing of the difference between Saul and David; and as he knew him to be the king's son-in-law, he wondered to see him come without any attendants.
entries.1b7b79872a1554d6f6d50b9c5281c724109284c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10321" type="x-p"/> The king hath commanded me a business - All said here is an untruth, and could not be dictated by the Spirit of the Lord; but there is no reason to believe that David was under the influence of Divine inspiration at this time. It is well known that from all antiquity it was held no crime to tell a lie, in order to save life. Thus Diphilus: - Ὑπολαμβανω το ψευδος επι σωτηριᾳ Λεγομενον, ουδεν περιποιεισθαι δυσχερες. "I hold it right to tell a lie, in order to procure my personal safety; nothing should be avoided in order to save life." <div eID="gen10321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10322" type="x-p"/> A heathen may say or sing thus; but no Christian can act thus, and save his soul, though he by doing so may save his life.
entries.6c27486f573b137786476b27cb59092f607486b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10323" type="x-p"/> So the priest gave him hallowed bread - To this history our Lord alludes, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.25">Mar 2:25</reference>, in order to show that in cases of absolute necessity a breach of the ritual law was no sin. It was lawful for the priests only to eat the shew-bread; but David and his companions were starving, no other bread could be had at the time, and therefore he and his companions ate of it without sin.
entries.ba1433f682a1f4b32b89060a4aca804b1bee2f1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10324" type="x-p"/> Detained before the Lord - Probably fulfilling some vow to the Lord, and therefore for a time resident at the tabernacle. <div eID="gen10324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10325" type="x-p"/> And his name was Doeg - From <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sam 22:9</reference> we learn that this man betrayed David's secret to Saul, which caused him to destroy the city, and slay eighty-five priests. We learn from its title that the fifty-second Psalm was made on this occasion; but titles are not to be implicitly trusted.
entries.285b0e8d655478fbfd15d7b0f66d6557069a87c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10326" type="x-p"/> The sword of Goliath - It has already been conjectured (see 1 Samuel 17:1-58) that the sword of Goliath was laid up as a trophy in the tabernacle.
entries.b94a9f5f487c910c72a0daea5e74aa25431c5a0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10327" type="x-p"/> Went to Achish the king of Gath - This was the worst place to which he could have gone: it was the very city of Goliath, whom he had slain, and whose sword he now wore; and he soon found, from the conversation of the servants of Achish, that his life was in the most imminent danger in this place.
entries.fa98d3d1a114baa1df625562dbc329f171b7e4d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10328" type="x-p"/> And he changed his behavior - Some imagine David was so terrified at the danger to which he was now exposed, that he was thrown into a kind of frenzy, accompanied with epileptic fits. This opinion is countenanced by the Septuagint, who render the passage thus: Ιδου ιδετε ανδρα επιλητον; "Behold, ye see an epileptic man. Why have ye introduced him to me?" Μη ελαττουμαι επιληπτων εγω; "Have I any need of epileptics, that ye have brought him to have his fits before me, (επιληπτευεσθαι προς με?") It is worthy of remark, that the spittle falling upon the beard, i.e., slavering or frothing at the mouth, is a genuine concomitant of an epileptic fit. <div eID="gen10328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10329" type="x-p"/> If this translation be allowed, it will set the conduct of David in a clearer point of view than the present translation does. But others think the whole was a feigned conduct, and that he acted the part of a lunatic or madman in order to get out of the hands of Achish and his courtiers. Many vindicate this conduct of David; but if mocking be catching, according to the proverb, he who feigns himself to be mad may, through the just judgment of God, become so. I dare not be the apologist of insincerity or lying. Those who wish to look farther into this subject may consult Dr. Chandler, Mr. Saurin, and Ortlob, in the first volume of Dissertations, at the end of the Dutch edition of the Critici Sacri.
entries.bd838373b8cc288891d6d47d94bc57ea7dc6a1da: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen10329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10330" type="x-p"/> Shall this fellow come into my house? - I will not take into my service a man who is liable to so grievous a disease. Chandler, who vindicates David's feigning himself, mad, concludes thus: "To deceive the deceiver is in many instances meritorious, in none criminal. And what so likely to deceive as the very reverse of that character which they had so misconstrued? He was undone as a wise man, he had a chance to escape as a madman; he tried, and the experiment succeeded." I confess I can neither feel the force nor the morality of this. Deceit and hypocrisy can never be pleasing in the sight of God.  <chapter eID="1Sam.21"/> <div eID="gen10330" type="x-p"/>

entries.4bb5ba952c0e6258f4a0f74123cfb5d7ccb4278d: <div eID="gen4036" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">David’s Flight to Nob, and Thence to Gath - <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.15">1Sa 21:1-15</reference></title> <div sID="gen4037" type="x-p"/> After the information which David had received from Jonathan, nothing remained for him in order to save his life but immediate flight. He could not return to the prophets at Ramah, where he had been miraculously preserved from the first outbreak of Saul’s wrath, because they could not ensure him permanent protection against the death with which he was threatened. He therefore fled first of all to Nob, to Ahimelech the high priest, to inquire the will of God through him concerning his future course (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.10">1Sa 22:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.15">1Sa 22:15</reference>), and induced him to give him bread and the sword of Goliath, also, under the pretext of having to perform a secret commission from the king with the greatest speed; for which Saul afterwards took fearful vengeance upon the priests at Nob when he was made acquainted with the affair through the treachery of Doeg (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.9">1Sa 21:1-9</reference>). David then fled to Gath to the Philistian king Achish; but here he was quickly recognised as the conqueror of Goliath, and obliged to feign insanity in order to save his life, and then to flee still farther (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15">1Sa 21:10-15</reference>). The state of his mind at this time he poured out before God in the words of <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1-Ps.56.13">Psa 56:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1-Ps.52.9">Psa 52:1-9</reference>, and 34. <div eID="gen4037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4038" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.2">1Sa 21:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">David at Nob</hi>. - The town of <hi type="italic">Nob</hi> or <hi type="italic">Nobeh</hi> (unless indeed the form נבה stands for נבה here and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sa 22:9</reference>, and the ה attached is merely ה local, as the name is always written נב in other places: vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.11">1Sa 22:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1">1Sa 21:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">Isa 10:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.32">Neh 11:32</reference>) was at that time a priests’ city (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:19</reference>), in which, according to the following account, the tabernacle was then standing, and the legal worship carried on. According to <reference osisRef="Isa.10.30">Isa 10:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">Isa 10:32</reference>, it was between Anathoth (<hi type="italic">Anata</hi>) and Jerusalem, and in all probability it has been preserved in the village of <hi type="italic">el-Isawiyeh</hi>, i.e., probably the village of Esau or Edom, which is midway between Anata and Jerusalem, an hour from the latter, and the same distance to the south-east of Gibeah of Saul (Tell el Phul), and which bears all the marks of an ancient place, partly in its dwellings, the stones of which date from a great antiquity, and partly in many marble columns which are found there (vid., <hi type="italic">Tobler</hi>, <hi type="italic">Topogr. v. Jerusalem</hi> ii. p. 720). Hence v. Raumer (<hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. p. 215, ed. 4) follows Kiepert in the map which he has appended to <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>'s <hi type="italic">Biblical Researches</hi>, and set down this place as the ancient <hi type="italic">Nob</hi>, for which <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi> indeed searched in vain (see <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 150). Ahimelech, the son of Ahitub, most probably the same person as Ahiah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference>), was “<hi type="italic">the priest</hi>,” i.e., the high priest (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference>). When David came to him, the priest “<hi type="italic">went trembling to meet him</hi>” (לקראת יחרד) with the inquiry, “<hi type="italic">Why art thou alone, and no one is with thee?</hi>” The unexpected appearance of David, the son-in-law of the king, without any attendants, alarmed Ahimelech, who probably imagined that he had come with a commission from the king which might involve him in danger. David had left the few servants who accompanied him in his flight somewhere in the neighbourhood, as we may gather from <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.2">1Sa 21:2</reference>, because he wished to converse with the high priest alone. Ahimelech’s anxious inquiry led David to resort to the fabrication described in <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.2">1Sa 21:2</reference> : “<hi type="italic">The king hath commanded me a business, and said to me, No one is to know anything of this matter, in which</hi> (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. in relation to the matter with regard to which) <hi type="italic">I send thee, and which I have entrusted to thee</hi> (i.e., no one is to know either the occasion or the nature of the commission): <hi type="italic">and the servants I have directed to such and such a place</hi>.” יודע, <hi type="italic">Poel</hi>, to cause to know, point, show. Ahimelech had received no information as yet concerning the most recent occurrences between Saul and David; and David would not confess to him that he was fleeing from Saul, because he was evidently afraid that the high priest would not give him any assistance, lest he should draw down the wrath of the king. This falsehood brought he greatest calamities upon Ahimelech and the priests at Nob (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.19">1Sa 22:9-19</reference>), and David was afterwards obliged to confess that he had occasioned it all (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.22">1Sa 22:22</reference>).
entries.a9e16dc85db79fee885033311c77a57a4bd42227: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.3">1Sa 21:3</reference> <div eID="gen4038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4039" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And now what is under thy hand? give into my hand</hi> (i.e., hand me) <hi type="italic">five loaves, or whatever</hi> (else) <hi type="italic">is to be found</hi>.” David asked for five loaves, because he had spoken of several attendants, and probably wanted to make provision for two or three days (Thenius).
entries.bc9ff7dd51a6f02f246ecd4ef543dc8ec02d8a68: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.4">1Sa 21:4</reference> <div eID="gen4039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4040" type="x-p"/> The priest answered that he had no common bread, but only holy bread, viz., according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.6">1Sa 21:6</reference>, shew-bread that had been removed, which none but priests were allowed to eat, and that in a sacred place; but that he was willing to give him some of these loaves, as David had said that he was travelling upon an important mission from the king, provided only that “<hi type="italic">the young men had kept themselves at least from women</hi>,” i.e., had not been defiled by sexual intercourse (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.18">Lev 15:18</reference>). If they were clean at any rate in this respect, he would in such a case of necessity depart from the Levitical law concerning the eating of the shew-bread, for the sake of observing the higher commandment of love to a neighbour (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Lev 19:18</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.12.5-Matt.12.6">Mat 12:5-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.2.25-Mark.2.26">Mar 2:25-26</reference>).<note placement="foot">When Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.26">Mar 2:26</reference>) assigns this action to the days of Abiathar the high priest, the statement rests upon an error of memory, in which Ahimelech is confounded with Abiathar.</note>
entries.bb0ceeccda5c476bf181ae9a6fa95cc9527ed7c3: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.5">1Sa 21:5</reference> <div eID="gen4040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4041" type="x-p"/> David quieted him concerning this scruple, and said, “<hi type="italic">Nay, but women have been kept from us since yesterday and the day before</hi>.” The use of אם כּי may be explained from the fact, that in David’s reply he paid more attention to the sense than to the form of the priest’s scruple, and expressed himself as concisely as possible. The words, “if the young men have only kept themselves from women,” simply meant, if only they are not unclean; and David replied, That is certainly not the case, <hi type="italic">but</hi> women have been kept from us; so that אם כּי has the meaning <hi type="italic">but</hi> in this passage also, as it frequently has after a previous negative, which is implied in the thought here as in 2Sa 13:33. “<hi type="italic">When I came out, the young men’s things were holy</hi> (Levitically clean); <hi type="italic">and if it is an unholy way, it becomes even holy through the instrument</hi>.” David does not say that the young men were clean when he came out (for the rendering given to הנּערים כּלי in the Septuagint, πάντα τὰ παιδάρια, is without any critical value, and is only a mistaken attempt to explain the word כּלי, which was unintelligible to the translator), but simply affirms that קדשׁ הנּערים כּלי, i.e., according to Luther’s rendering (<hi type="italic">der Knaben Zeug war heilig</hi>), the young men’s things (clothes, etc.) were holy. כּלים does not mean merely vessels, arms, or tools, but also the dress (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.5">Deu 22:5</reference>), or rather the clothes as well as such things as were most necessary to meet the wants of life. By the <hi type="italic">coitus</hi>, or strictly speaking, by the <hi type="italic">emissio seminis</hi> in connection with the <hi type="italic">coitus</hi>, not only were the persons themselves defiled, but also every article of clothing or leather upon which any of the <hi type="italic">semen</hi> fell (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.18">Lev 15:18</reference>); so that it was necessary for the purpose of purification that the things which a man had on should all be washed. David explains, with evident allusion to this provision, that the young men’s things were holy, i.e., perfectly clean, for the purpose of assuring the priest that there was not the smallest Levitical uncleanness attaching to them. The clause which follows is to be taken as conditional, and as supposing a possible case: “<hi type="italic">and if it is an unholy way</hi>.” דּרך, the way that David was going with his young men, i.e., his purpose of enterprise, by which, however, we are not to understand his request of holy bread from Ahimelech, but the performance of the king’s commission of which he had spoken. כּי ואף, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. besides (there is) also that, = moreover there is also the fact, that it becomes holy through the instrument; i.e., as <hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi> has correctly explained it, “on the supposition of the important royal mission, upon which David pretended to be sent, <hi type="italic">through</hi> <hi type="italic">me</hi> as an ambassador of the anointed of the Lord,” in which, at any rate, David’s meaning really was, “the way was sanctified before God, when he, as His chosen servant, the preserver of the true kingdom of God in Israel, went to him in his extremity.” That פּלי in the sense of instrument is also applied to <hi type="italic">men</hi>, is evident from <reference osisRef="Isa.13.5">Isa 13:5</reference> and Jer 50:25.
entries.8efe3a2e4a2d6381a636a4b15c2b78e358d5717a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.6-1Sam.21.7">1Sa 21:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen4041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4042" type="x-p"/> The priest then gave him (what was) holy, namely the shew-loaves “<hi type="italic">that were taken from before Jehovah</hi>,” i.e., from the holy table, upon which they had lain before Jehovah for seven days (vid., <reference osisRef="Lev.24.6-Lev.24.9">Lev 24:6-9</reference>). - In <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.7">1Sa 21:7</reference> there is a parenthetical remark introduced, which was of great importance in relation to the consequences of this occurrence. There at the sanctuary there was a man of Saul’s servants, נעצר, i.e., “<hi type="italic">kept back</hi> (shut off) <hi type="italic">before Jehovah</hi>:” i.e., at the sanctuary of the tabernacle, either for the sake of purification or as a proselyte, who wished to be received into the religious communion of Israel, or because of supposed leprosy, according to Lev 13:4. His name was Doeg the Edomite, הרעים אבּיר, “<hi type="italic">the strong one</hi> (i.e., the overseer) <hi type="italic">of the herdsmen of Saul</hi>.”<note placement="foot">The Septuagint translators have rendered these words νέμων τὰς ἡμιόνους, “feeding the mules of Saul;” and accordingly in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sa 22:9</reference> also they have changed Saul’s servants into mules, in accordance with which Thenius makes Doeg the upper herdsman of Saul. But it is very evident that the text of the lxx is nothing more than a subjective interpretation of the expression before us, and does not presuppose any other text, from the simple fact that all the other ancient versions are founded upon the Hebrew text both here and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sa 22:9</reference>, including even the Vulgate (<hi type="italic">potentissimus pastorum</hi>); and the clause contained in some of the MSS of the Vulgate (<hi type="italic">his pascebat mulas Saul</hi>) is nothing more than a gloss that has crept in from the Itala; and this is still more obvious in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.9">1Sa 22:9</reference>, where נצּב והוּא is applicable enough to עבדי, but is altogether unsuitable in connection with פרדי, since נצּב is no more applied in Hebrew to herdsmen or keepers of animals, than we should think of speaking of presidents of asses, horses, etc. Moreover, it is not till the reign of David that we read of mules being used as riding animals by royal princes (<reference osisRef="2Sam.13.29">2Sa 13:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.9">2Sa 18:9</reference>); and they are mentioned for the first time as beasts of burden, along with asses, camels, and oxen, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.40">1Ch 12:40</reference>, where they are said to have been employed by the northern tribes to carry provisions to Hebron to the festival held at the recognition of David as king. Before David’s time the sons of princes rode upon asses (vid., Jdg 10:4; Jdg 12:14).</note>
entries.709096dd2a63f43e7e9d59de2a4c6c41a1bf42e9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.8">1Sa 21:8</reference> <div eID="gen4042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4043" type="x-p"/> David also asked Ahimelech whether he had not a sword or a javelin at hand; “<hi type="italic">for I have neither brought my sword nor my</hi> (other) <hi type="italic">weapons with me, because the affair of the king was pressing</hi>,” i.e., very urgent, נחוּץ, ἁπ. λεγ., literally, compressed.
entries.5e3ab84558691a80343943e6415da141ddbdbe26: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.9">1Sa 21:9</reference> <div eID="gen4043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4044" type="x-p"/> The priest replied, that there was only the sword of Goliath, whom David slew in the terebinth valley (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.2">1Sa 17:2</reference>), wrapped up in a cloth hanging behind the ephod (the high priest’s shoulder-dress), - a sign of the great worth attached to this dedicatory offering. He could take that. David accepted it, as a weapon of greater value to him than any other, because he had not only taken this sword as booty from the Philistine, but had cut off the head of Goliath with it (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.51">1Sa 17:51</reference>). When and how this sword had come into the tabernacle is not known (see the remarks on <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.54">1Sa 17:54</reference>). The form בּזּה for בּזה is only met with here. On the <hi type="italic">Piska</hi>, see at Jos 4:1.
entries.441b48496dccc0ee0789c070bcf9c6b1a64e98d0: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.11">1Sa 21:10-11</reference> <hi type="italic">David with Achish at Gath</hi>. - David fled from Nob to Achish of Gath. This Philistian king is called <hi type="italic">Abimelech</hi> in the heading of Ps 34, according to the standing title of the Philistian princes at Gath. The fact that David fled at once out of the land, and that to the Philistines at Gath, may be accounted for from the great agitation into which he had been thrown by the information he had received from Jonathan concerning Saul’s implacable hatred. As some years had passed since the defeat of Goliath, and the conqueror of Goliath was probably not personally known to many of the Philistines, he might hope that he should not be recognised in Gath, and that he might receive a welcome there with his few attendants, as a fugitive who had been driven away by Saul, the leading foe of the Philistines.<note placement="foot">This removes the objection raised by modern critics to the historical credibility of the narrative before us, namely, that David would certainly not have taken refuge at once with the Philistines, but would only have gone to them in the utmost extremity (Thenius). It is impossible to see how the words “he fled <hi type="italic">that day for fear of Saul</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.11">1Sa 21:11</reference>) are to prove that this section originally stood in a different connection, and are only arbitrarily inserted here (Thenius). Unless we tear away the words in the most arbitrary manner from the foregoing word ויּברח, they not only appear quite suitable, but even necessary, since David’s journey to Abimelech was not a flight, or at all events it is not described as a flight in the text; and David’s flight from Saul really began with his departure from Nob. Still less can the legendary origin of this account be inferred from the fact that some years afterwards David really did take refuge with Achish in the Philistian country (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1-1Sam.27.12">1Sa 27:1-12</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1-1Sam.29.11">1Sa 29:1-11</reference>), or the conjecture sustained that this is only a distorted legend of that occurrence. For if the later sojourn of David with Achish be a historical fact, that popular legend could not possibly have assumed a form so utterly different as the account before us, to say nothing of the fact that this occurrence has a firm historical support in Psa 34:1.</note> <div eID="gen4044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4045" type="x-p"/> But in this he was mistaken. He was recognised at once by the courtiers of Achish. They said to their prince, “<hi type="italic">Is not this David the king of the land? Have they not sung in circles, Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands?</hi>” (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6-1Sam.18.7">1Sa 18:6-7</reference>). “<hi type="italic">King of the land</hi>” they call David, not because his anointing and divine election were known to them, but on account of his victorious deeds, which had thrown Saul entirely into the shade. Whether they intended by these words to celebrate David as a hero, or to point him out to their prince as a dangerous man, cannot be gathered from the words themselves, nor can the question be decided with certainty at all (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.5">1Sa 29:5</reference>).
entries.fa5f0de83976548b65e17712f5305d0885dfd0da: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.12-1Sam.21.13">1Sa 21:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen4045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4046" type="x-p"/> But David took these words to heart, and was in great fear of Achish, lest he should treat him as an enemy, and kill him. In order to escape this danger, “<hi type="italic">he disguised his understanding</hi> (i.e., pretended to be out of his mind) <hi type="italic">in their eyes</hi> (i.e., before the courtiers of Achish), <hi type="italic">behaved insanely under their hands</hi> (when they tried to hold him as a madman), <hi type="italic">scribbled upon the door-wings, and let his spittle run down into his beard</hi>.” The suffix to וישׁנּו is apparently superfluous, as the object, את־טעמו, follows immediately afterwards. But it may be accounted for from the circumstantiality of the conversation of every-day life, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.6">2Sa 14:6</reference>, and (though these cases are not perfectly parallel) <reference osisRef="Exod.2.6">Exo 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">Pro 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">Eze 10:3</reference> (cf. <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi>' <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. §121, 6, Anm. 3). ויתו, from תּוה, to make signs, i.e., to scribble. The lxx and Vulgate render it ἐτυμπανίζειν, <hi type="italic">impingebat</hi>, <hi type="italic">he drummed</hi>, smote with his fists upon the wings of the door, which would make it appear as if they had read ויּתף (from תּפף), which seems more suitable to the condition of a madman whose saliva ran out of his mouth.
entries.b6788b45cf8c593fbbcdf021c79b482ac4990494: <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.14-1Sam.21.15">1Sa 21:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen4046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4047" type="x-p"/> By this dissimulation David escaped the danger which threatened him; for Achish thought him mad, and would have nothing to do with him. “<hi type="italic">Wherefore do ye bring him to me? Have I need of madmen, that ye have brought this man hither to rave against me?</hi> <hi type="italic">Shall this man come into my house?</hi>” Thus Achish refused to receive him into his house. But whether he had David taken over the border, or at any rate out of the town; or whether David went away of his own accord; or whether he was taken away by his servants, and then hurried as quickly as possible out of the land of the Philistines, is not expressly mentioned, as being of no importance in relation to the principal object of the narrative. All that is stated is, that he departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam.  <chapter eID="1Sam.21"/> <div eID="gen4047" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ And David said unto Ahimelech, And is there not here under thine hand spear or sword? for I have neither brought my sword, nor my weapons with me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">These he left behind him, that he might with less suspi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion remove from place to place, and hide himself from Saul and his Spies.</ns0:note>, because the kings business required haste <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Message came to me, when I was un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />armed, and the business required so great expedition that I could not go home to fetch my Weapons.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And the Priest said, The sword of Goliah the Philistine, whom thou slewest in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17. 2.</ns0:note> the valley of Elah, behold, it <ns0:hi>is here</ns0:hi> wrapt in a cloth behind the Ephod <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Behind that Holy place allotted for the keeping of the Sacred, or Priestly Garments; all which are here comprehended under the <ns0:hi>Ephod;</ns0:hi> which, as the chief of the kind, is put for all the rest. Here it was laid up as a Sacred Monument of God's Power and Goodness, and that famous Victory, related <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 17.</ns0:note>: if thou wilt take that, take <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no other save that, here. Qu.</ns0:hi> But why did he go to these, and not rather to some other neighbour Nation? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they were all at Peace with <ns0:hi>Saul;</ns0:hi> and therefore would certainly have delivered him up, upon <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Demands.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p>And the servants of Achish said unto him, <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> not this David the king of the land <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of this land; i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the Land of <ns0:hi>Canaan.</ns0:hi> They call him <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> either more generally for the Governour, as that Word is used, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 5. for the most eminent Captain and Commander, and, as it were the King of the <ns0:hi>Israelitish</ns0:hi> Armies: or, rather more specially, <ns0:hi>the king;</ns0:hi> to wit, The King Elect, the Person designed to be King: for by this time, the Fame of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Rejection, and <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Destination to the Kingdom, was got abroad among the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and from them, probably to the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> ears.</ns0:note>? did they not sing one to another of him in dances, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 18. 7.</ns0:note> Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">And therefore con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sider what to do; and now thine, and our great Enemy is in thy hand, be sure thou never let him go alive.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And David laid up these words in his heart, and was sore afraid <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Lest either their Revenge or Policy should prompt them to kill him.</ns0:note> of Achish the king of Gath:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 34. title.</ns0:note> he changed his behaviour <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">His Speech and Gesture; and, it may be, his Habit also.</ns0:note> before them, and feigned himself mad <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which they might the more easily believe; partly, became of the disappointment of his great hopes, and his extream danger and trouble from <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> which might well make him mad: and partly, because he had put himself into their hands; which they supposed, none but a Fool, or a Mad-man would have done.
